posts.content:
Every time a robot makes a mistake, that's a learning opportunity. A lot of robots learn from successful demonstrations, but things don't always go perfectly (especially in the real world vs. a lab).

Our AI research team developed something called ValueFormer. It's a critic model that helps our bi-manual robot realize when it's not doing well. Rather than just learning from successes, ValueFormer learns from mistakes and human interventions and gives real-time feedback (something we were missing with behavior cloning alone).

The early results look promising: in a run where the robot needed to assemble two burgers in a row (which is more difficult because the second burger assembly doesn't start with perfectly stacked ingredients), two different critic-derived training approaches improved successful completion from 70% to 85%.

I'm excited about this because it's another way robots can continuously improve in production. Our data flywheel learns from successful executions, and now ValueFormer learns from failures and human takeovers. Link to our blog in comments!

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 month ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Pick food ingredients up from a pan. Place them into a tray. Repeat.

This sounds like the simplest thing a robot can do.

But on a production line, the trays never stop moving. The conveyor keeps running, constantly accelerating and decelerating while the robot is in motion, so by the time the robot arm arrives, the target tray has moved. 

If the robot pauses between picking and placing to recalculate the ideal deposit location, it falls behind. Production lines don't wait.

To solve this, we created a motion-planning stack that generates trajectories for picking and placing separately and then merges them in real time. This merged state matches the joint position and velocity at the exact handoff point, so the arm transitions smoothly from one motion to the next without stopping.

On top of that, an adaptive timing layer continuously forecasts where each moving tray will be at a future point and recalculates the robot arm's trajectory in real time, learning from prior cycles to arrive at exactly the right moment.

The result is a smooth, uninterrupted pick-and-place motion that keeps up with a conveyor that never stops.

posts.content:
Testing on-device software that runs on physical hardware is one of those problems that sounds straightforward until you're actually trying to do it.

Chef's conveyor companion box manages the deposit-and-go sequence on stop-and-go production lines. Every robot on the line has to finish its deposit before the conveyor moves again. The box coordinates all of that. Getting it wrong means synchronization races, missed deposits, and bugs that only show up on a live customer line.

We had two ways to test this logic without hardware. Neither covered the full loop.
- The first was unit tests. They never ran the actual runner or the cycle loop, which is exactly where timing bugs live. 
- The second was a manual workflow that still required a physical RevPi. Neither was good enough.

So our team built a hardware abstraction layer within the runner and an in-process PLC model to simulate the customer conveyor controller. The complete indexing stack now runs on a developer laptop with zero hardware in the loop.

The interesting part about this problem was that it had two independent layers of hardware coupling, and fixing one without the other still left the stack unable to run end-to-end. The solution only worked when both were solved together.

Read more about how we built this on our engineering blog (link in comments)!

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
One of the hardest problems in physical AI is something that sounds simple: adding a new ingredient.

In reality, it’s not.

Every ingredient behaves differently. Some compress, some stick, some spill, some drip. Choosing the right utensil (and how to move it) can have a big impact on yield, speed, and reliability. Historically, onboarding new ingredients to ChefOS required experienced engineers to reason through all of this manually.

We tried a straightforward approach first: match new ingredients to similar ones using embeddings. It didn’t work because what looks similar isn’t necessarily manipulated the same way.

So our AI team built SAGE, an LLM agent that reasons through ingredient behavior, selects the right utensils, pulls from production data, and recommends how our robots should handle new ingredients.

LLMs are useful here because they combine structured production data with qualitative reasoning and capture how ingredients actually behave, not just how they look. They also let us encode expert heuristics and iterate fast without retraining our models.

This was an exciting engineering challenge for our team to solve, and a good example of how physical AI systems can adapt to the messy, unstructured environments they need to operate in.

Read more about how we built SAGE on our engineering blog (link in comments)!

posts.content:
Three years ago, we had one robot in one facility in the US.

Today, Chef robots run in production at scale across North America and Europe.

Here's what surprised me most about building this: the fix for a growing robot fleet isn't more support staff. It's a layered system that catches most issues before a person ever needs to.

The first layer is the robot fixing itself. We used to get 4 am calls because a conveyor got bumped and the robots weren't flush anymore. Now our autonomy stack automatically re-registers with the conveyor to correct itself without requiring a call. We've built autonomy for hundreds of situations like this, and every time something new comes up, we ask the same question: can the robot solve this itself next time?

The second layer is telling the user before they even notice. If the robot can't fix something on its own, like a conveyor running faster than it can keep up with, our software flags it directly so the user can act immediately.

The third layer is 24/7 remote support. Requests get triaged around the clock, so customer support never depends on time zones. We have invested heavily in data pipelines and data infrastructure to allow us to have all the data to triage. Our engineers debug live robots remotely with tools like Foxglove, and customers can page us anytime for urgent issues.

The fourth layer is the time when hardware needs physical attention. In that case, a network of certified third-party technicians handles routine repairs, and our engineers travel on-site for larger integrations.

None of this works without testing it before it reaches the field. We run our software through SIL, HIL, and continuous integration testing because catching an issue in the lab is better than catching it at 4 am in a customer's facility.

The result: our support headcount is growing sublinearly to the number of robots we deploy. Customers are scaling with us without our support team scaling at the same rate. One customer went from 2 robots to 36. Another from 2 to 22. Another from 4 to 20. Another from 3 to 12.

That's the model. More on how we built it is in the blog. Link in comments.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 week ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
An experienced food assembly line worker doesn't pick ingredients from a bin the same way on day one as they do after six months.

Our robots now do the same thing.

We built a 6D sparse failure maps feature for reactive pick learning.

This is an on-device experience model that records every failed ingredient pick from the bin across the full 6-DoF action space—position, depth, approach angle, and gripper twist. The model updates continuously as the robot operates, adapting in real time to the specific characteristics of every site, system, and SKU it runs on. 

Before each pick, the planner queries this learned memory and steers the robot away from pose regions that have already proven unreliable on that line, ensuring the robot picks from the best possible spot every time.

In the visualization below, the red markers represent failed pick poses that the robot has logged. The blue arrow indicates where the planner sends the robot instead, towards the most reliable pick available.

As a result, the physical AI model becomes more reliable the longer it runs on a given line. That's not just because of fleet-wide training, but because it's building a failure map that makes each ingredient pick more precise.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
We started building a world model for food.

Food is a uniquely difficult robotics problem because it's deformable, granular, sticky, viscous, temperature-dependent, ... (the list goes on), and no two batches of the same food behave exactly the same. Traditional physics simulators struggle with that complexity.

Because our robots have already made more than 130 million servings in production, we can use this data to train our Food World Model (FWM) to predict how much food a robot will pick and what the pan will look like after the pick. 

In our initial run, the FWM improved overall weight-prediction error from 13.6 g to 10.3 g and reduced post-pick surface error by 42%.

With FWM, can take the outcome of each candidate action, then choose per pan state instead of applying one recipe to every state. Among equal-mean actions, take the one with the lowest predicted spread. Said another way, we can simulate thousands of possible actions with different parameters and then actually execute the action with the lowest standard deviation. This will result in much better consistency and thus ROI for customers. 

Further, a new ingredient becomes finding an embedding and optimizing over tools and parameters inside the world model. 

For Chef, we don't use any video pre-training. The entire FWM dataset is 100% production data. And the result is there's no sim-2-real gap; it's all prod data. 

Read our blog (link in comments) that comes with an interactive visualization of our FWM predictions!

postedAt.postedAgoText: 2 weeks ago • Edited • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Placing food into tray inserts sounds simple, but our robots need to know both where the insert is and how it's oriented - two different challenges that our robots need to solve simultaneously.

To detect inserts, we use an AI model that draws an oriented bounding box (OBB) around each insert in the camera image. The challenge is that our AI models can correctly identify where the insert is, yet still get the angle wrong. When the angle is off, the robot either spills or misses the deposit, and trying to correct mid-motion only makes it worse, risking a hit to the insert wall or dropping food in the wrong spot.

Getting the angle right is harder than it sounds. The same insert can be described with different angles, widths, and heights, which is the representation ambiguity problem with OBBs. And for nearly-square inserts, simply comparing two angles can report a large error when the orientations are actually nearly identical, because the angle wraps around at the edges of the range.

To fix this, we've built a review tool that converts all OBB angle labels to a single, consistent range so reviews and debugging always compare orientations in the same format the model uses. It also handles the wraparound cases correctly, so we're not penalizing labels that are actually fine.

We also added an angle-training gain, making angular accuracy directly part of the AI model's training objective. But this comes with a trade-off: label quality matters much more now. An incorrect or inconsistent OBB angle in the training data becomes a stronger signal, not a weaker one. So the review tool also checks every label against its standardized angle, records human verdicts, and produces a report of labels that need fixing before angle-loss training begins.

posts.content:
People usually evaluate food assembly robots based on labor savings, throughput, or yield savings. Those are important, but there's another benefit we haven't talked about a lot: carbon emissions.

Every gram of food that doesn't need to be grown, processed, transported, or thrown away also prevents carbon emissions. When meal assembly robots reduce giveaway, improve consistency, minimize spillage, and prevent production runs from ending early because an ingredient runs out, manufacturers don't just lower costs, they also reduce carbon emissions from food production right at the source.

Given that food loss and waste account for roughly 8–10% of global greenhouse gas emissions, that's an impact worth paying attention to. 

We wrote a blog that breaks down the connection between robotic food assembly, giveaway cost savings (see graphic below), and emissions reduction (link in comments)!

posts.content:
The fascinating thing about robotics is that no problem is trivial.

Scooping a burrito bowl sounds easy until you try to make a robot do it: rice clumps differently in every scoop. Beans sit in liquid. Cheese sticks together. Lettuce shifts around. A tiny motion that feels natural to humans can cause spills, inaccurate portions, or cross-contamination.

What makes this especially interesting is that burgers and burrito bowls require fundamentally different manipulation strategies:
• Burgers are assembled from discrete objects
• Burrito bowls involve scooping loose, deformable materials with precise portioning

In our latest engineering blog, we talk about how we taught the same Food Foundation Model (FFM) that could already stack a burger to now scoop burrito bowls.

We didn’t redesign the robotics stack or hand-engineer a new system. Instead, we kept the same physical AI architecture and trained the model on new demonstrations of people assembling burrito bowls.

We also built a robot-friendly handle that lets our robot use ordinary kitchen utensils. This reduces a huge amount of grasp variation.

After 25 hours of demonstrations, our robot achieved a 95% success rate.

One of the things I find most exciting about physical AI is that every “simple” real-world task forces you to confront incredibly subtle manipulation problems. Our work never gets boring!

Full blog in comments.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 2 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Every time you open an instant noodle bowl, there's a seasoning sachet inside. Maybe there's also a sauce pouch, a garnish packet, and a small cutlery kit. 

Someone put those there - a human. 

Our robots can now automate the manual and repetitive work of placing sachets and kits into these bowls. And not just for noodle bowls - think picking and placing discrete items such as sauce sachets, seasoning packets, garnish toppers, dried proteins, foil-sealed pouches, plastic-wrapped cutlery kits, and desiccant packets into cups, bowls, trays, and packaging containers before sealing. 

This covers a significant share of what goes through CPG production lines: ramen bowls, lunchable-style multi-compartment trays, global meal kits with a sauce pouch, naan, and a sauce packet tucked inside, premium snack cups with a topper, and any product that needs a cutlery drop. 

Almost all of it is still done by hand. Not because no one has tried to automate it, but because it's a genuinely hard problem.

These items are nothing like the raw ingredients our robots already handle. A cutlery pack is a bit stiffer. A dried shrimp packet is lighter. A desiccant packet looks nothing like the first two. Every item behaves differently and sits at a different angle in an unstructured bin after every pick. 

We spent a lot of time on this. 

Our physical AI models and computer vision assess each item's position, shape, and orientation in real time, determine how to pick the item without crumpling it, and place it precisely without damaging it. No pre-sorting or fixed bin arrangement required.

We also had to build placement logic for how these items actually need to land: some SKUs require a sachet to lie flat with the tear-notch facing a specific direction; some require multiple items to be placed in a single pass; some have compartments with different inserts in each section where nothing can migrate between sections.

The next time you tear open that seasoning sachet, there's a reasonable chance a robot put it there.

Read more on our blog (link in comments)!

posts.content:
One of the most captivating debates in robotics right now is the VLAs vs. world models one. Having worked with both, I don't think you need to pick a side.

At Chef, we use VLAs in our research work because they're the most practical way to learn complex food manipulation tasks from demonstrations right now. We've spent a lot of time adapting them to our specific use cases and solving challenges like latency that become very noticeable when you're controlling a real robot running on industry-specific hardware.

But I also think world models are where much of the long-term opportunity lies.

Food manipulation is fundamentally a physics problem. Rice behaves differently depending on how it was cooked. Mashed potatoes change in consistency when they cool down. Oatmeal, shredded chicken, and pasta deform in very different ways under the gripper movement. If a robot could run on an accurate predictive model of these dynamics and really understand "food physics," it could reason about outcomes and get it right every time rather than imitating demonstrations and failing in certain edge cases.

Our approach is to leverage both. 

This is an exciting time for robotics. Thanks to Rocket Drew and The Information for including us (link to article in comments)!

posts.content:
AI is all over the job market news right now, but we're only starting to understand how it's actually affecting our work.

In tech, individuals and teams are becoming 100x more efficient. 

But in the food industry, AI is actually instrumental in keeping production going. Over 1.1 million food industry jobs went unfilled in 2023 - a labor shortage that has forced food manufacturers to leave demand unmet or even move their production offshore.

Physical AI is solving this labor shortage by automating the most repetitive, difficult-to-staff jobs. Instead of replacing jobs and fueling job anxiety, it's a solution to a problem that had kept food manufacturers worried for years.

This is just one example of how AI is affecting every industry differently, and it's the beginning of a big shift in the labor market that will affect most jobs out there (mine included).

What's next after meatpacking and produce packing? It's baked goods.

Burger buns, chocolate chip cookies, biscotti, butter cookies, biscuits, fortune cookies, granola bars, rusks, shortbreads, and many other baked items... Chef robots can now automate tray assembly for all of these.

Every item behaves differently on the production line. A granola bar can warp when gripped incorrectly. A rusk can crack if picked at the wrong angle. A butter cookie can crumble if the utensil's suction isn't calibrated correctly. And each baked item needs to be placed in a tray or packaging container that looks exactly right, as shelf appeal is non-negotiable for retail-ready baked goods packaging.

So we weren't just solving a picking-and-placing problem. We were solving a problem where the margin for error is essentially zero at production speed across dozens of SKUs that all behave differently.

We built baked goods packing on top of our existing piece-picking capability. Chef robots use our physical AI models to assess each item's position, shape, and orientation in real time, reorient it mid-motion after picking, and place it on the tray exactly where it needs to land.

Whether it’s a burger bun that needs to be placed flat side down, shortbreads that need to be arranged at a uniform angle, or multiple cookies that need to be stacked into each compartment to the exact count, our robots can handle these requirements in a single automated pass.

Every capability we add frees up workers from repetitive, physically demanding tasks for less repetitive, more meaningful work.

I’m excited to show off some of the work that our AI team has been working on! 

We’re building a bi-manual food prep system powered by our Food Foundation Model (FFM) that can handle high-complexity and high-dexterity prep table food assembly (think burgers, sandwiches, burrito bowls) rather than just conveyor-belt assembly. 

What’s exciting is that this system learns from human demonstration rather than being programmed. What this means is that the system can perform human-like motions that would be next to impossible to program. 

This is key since prep tables aren’t structured. They’re messy, variable, and require a single worker to assemble an entire meal from start to finish. But prep tables are how the majority of food gets assembled. That’s why a big part of the food industry still depends on manual labor.

We knew we needed to build the FFM because off-the-shelf VLAs and physical AI models weren’t good enough for food manipulation. Most VLAs are trained on rigid-body manipulation, but food manipulation deals with highly variable, deformable materials (think wet, sticky, and irregularly shaped).

Relative to our current robots in production, which use many different physical AI models for tasks like detecting trays, scooping food, and picking individual items, our FFM will handle everything in a single model and quickly extend to new tasks.

This is exciting since it’ll unlock physical AI deployments in ghost kitchens, fast-casual restaurants, airline catering, schools, hospitals, military, prisons, stadiums, corporate dining, and hotels.

We also expect some emergent characteristics from our FFM, for example, zero-shot or few-shot ingredient onboarding, adapting to new ingredients with minimal training. The model will also self-improve and autonomously increase yield and consistency over time.

It’ll also work on cross-embodied hardware. In the video below, you can see the FFM working with both our food-safe system and a research platform. 

Still early, but this feels like an important step toward making physical AI work all across the entire food industry! Read more on our blog (link in comments).

We’re excited to deploy physical AI into every commercial kitchen!

posts.content:
We've been building a physical AI system that assembles a burger in under a minute. Earlier, it hit 75% success rate. We just got it to 91.3%, and the way we did it says something interesting about how physical AI models actually get better.

The improvement didn't come from a bigger model or more demonstration hours. We added 56 successful burger assembly runs back into the training data. That's just 4.5% more data, and it improved our system's success rate by 16 points.

The reason comes down to how we trained the system in the first place.

We trained it on human demonstrations: operators guide both arms through the full burger assembly sequence on one hardware platform, and the model learns from those recordings. The problem is that our physical AI system runs on different hardware, which means the conditions the model was trained on and the conditions it operates in are never exactly the same: different lighting, ingredients that are arranged differently, and joint configurations it has never seen before. The moment the system hits something unfamiliar, small errors start to compound.

The 56 runs we added were recorded by our system under the exact conditions it operates under, covering the specific situations the system had been struggling with, in a way that human demonstrations never could.

We call this loop the data flywheel: every successful run becomes training data for the next version of the physical AI model. The more the system runs, the better the data and the model get. This 16-point jump came from a single iteration, and it's built to keep running.

Read more about how we built this—link in comments!

posts.content:
When Chef robots pick food from a pan, the pan changes constantly—ingredients shift, deplete unevenly, and clump differently depending on their type. A good pick location at the start of a shift is often a bad one just 15 minutes later.

Picking well means optimizing for many things at once: consistent volume across tools, collision avoidance, and cycle-time efficiency, among others.

Our pick-scoring pipeline meets these competing goals by composing a stack of independently tunable subscorers. Each one is a focused heuristic or physical AI model output that produces its own 2D heatmap over the pan. These subscorers are dynamic and adapt as the module runs. It leverages live perception data, on-device failure memory, and the system's own pick history to converge towards more consistent results per shift.

The image below shows what this looks like in practice: a pan of granola on the left and, on the right, a grid of heatmaps showing how different subscorers are scoring the same pan at the same moment. Red means a high score; blue means a low score. Each frame reflects a different signal that the system weighs before committing to a pick location.

The pick-scoring pipeline is what keeps pick quality consistent from the first scoop to the last, and our robots don't degrade as a pan empties. They adapt.

We're grateful to be in the Robots for America industry coalition and excited to see bipartisan momentum behind a proposed National Commission on Robotics. For years, we've talked about AI strategy, but it's time we start talking about robotics strategy too.

When policymakers evaluate robotics competitiveness, they should ask:
• How do we accelerate robot deployment in critical industries like manufacturing, food, logistics, healthcare?
• How do we make sure robotics datasets are created in the US?
• How do we teach the technicians, operators, and engineers needed to support large-scale deployment?
• How do we strengthen domestic robotics supply chains so we're not dependent on foreign competitors?

Robotics is becoming a strategic technology, and the countries that deploy robots at scale (not just invent them) will shape this industry.

posts.content:
When we built our physical AI system that assembles a burger in under a minute, we noticed something weird. The robot was shaky and wobbly.

We started measuring and found a pattern. The shaking was happening every 1.6 seconds, and it came down to the latency between our VLA predicting action chunks and the robot executing them. The VLA would tell the robot to carry out an action chunk, but by the time the robot finished executing it, the prediction was already stale.

This shaking problem had 3 causes:
1. Model inference delay: Our VLA takes time to run inference, so its observations are stale by the time the robot finishes executing.
2. Leader–follower mechanical lag: During teleoperated data collection, the follower robot tracks the leader, so the recorded joint state is always behind the commanded action.
3. Camera asynchrony: OS scheduling and bandwidth contention introduce jitter across cameras.

Once we understood where the delay was coming from, we needed to measure the combined latency from all three sources and shift the prediction target by exactly that amount.

Instead of waiting for each prediction before acting, we moved to asynchronous inference: we issued the next prediction earlier, before the current action chunk was fully executed.

With this latency compensation, we reduced velocity discontinuity by 64.9% and acceleration jerk by 30.8% on a real bimanual robot running at 30 Hz, with no additional inference cost.

posts.content:
Unlike language models, food manipulation has no internet-scale dataset. Ingredients are deformable, variable, wet, and sticky. The only way to build better models is to collect data from robots operating on real production lines.

Every serving a Chef robot makes teaches the next one. Our robots have assembled more than 120 million servings in production. Every pick, every placement, and every production run generates data that improves our physical AI models. We call this the data flywheel.

Over time, this production data has made Chef robots more reliable, expanded the ingredients they can handle, shortened onboarding for new foods, and accelerated deployment for new customers. This ultimately comes back to our customers, who see improved performance in ingredient coverage, throughput, consistency, and placement quality. 

Our models don't just learn from successful picks. They also learn from failed ones, recording unsuccessful pick positions, depths, approach angles, and gripper orientations to avoid those mistakes in the future.

It's also helping us build our Food Foundation Model, which we think will unlock entirely new applications for food robotics.

We wrote more about how the flywheel works and why we think production data is one of the biggest long-term advantages in physical AI (link in comments)!

posts.content:
When food manufacturers ask us about ROI, the conversation almost always starts with labor. That makes sense. Turnover in this industry regularly exceeds 150%, and a workstation costs far more than the wage on the paycheck once you add workers' comp, benefits, recruiting, and retraining.

But there's a second lever that's not as obvious right away: giveaway.

Every meal has a target weight. If a tray comes in under that weight, it's a compliance problem. If it comes in over, nobody complains. So what does a line worker do while scooping hundreds of portions an hour in a 32°F cold room? They end up adding extra grams to every tray: food a manufacturer produces, pays for, and then hands to the customer for free. 

Along with that, if workers over-scoop one ingredient for a few hours, it runs out before the batch is done, and the unfinished trays, along with everything staged for them, get thrown out too. 

And even if it doesn't sound like much, across millions of trays a year, it quietly eats a manufacturer's margin.

This is where Chef robots have a real advantage. Along with speed, Chef robots bring consistency. They deposit the same food portion from hour one to hour eight of a shift, tray after tray, with no fatigue and no reason to scoop extra. Customers running our robots have seen up to 88% less giveaway, and for many of them, it's the first place ROI becomes visible.

In addition to food giveaway, labor, production capacity, throughput, and safety are the other four ROI levers our robots bring to manufacturers. We broke down the full picture in our latest blog. Link in comments!

posts.content:
For the last decade, building robots largely meant writing code. Engineers specified trajectories, tuned heuristics, and programmed every behavior by hand. While there was a lot of machine learning, it was in modules that work together to accomplish the end task. 

Today, it's starting to look different with end-to-end policies (pixels in and controls out), and the quality of a system really depends on the quality of its training data. You could argue that robotics is becoming a data discipline.

We just wrote a blog on this transition to more end-to-end techniques and how they fit into the broader evolution of robotics.

It's interesting to look at the progression from mechatronic automation to programmed robots, learned heuristics, hybrid AI, and today's end-to-end learning systems. And it also explains why food robotics is a super challenging discipline: the real world is messy, and deformable materials are still incredibly difficult to simulate.

I hope this piece is useful to anyone trying to understand where robotics is today and where we're headed over the next few years. Link in comments!

postedAt.postedAgoText: 2 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Robotics has made so much progress, but still, some tasks are incredibly hard.

Robots can follow natural-language instructions, generalize to new tasks, and do increasingly complex manipulation.

Bimanual manipulation is one of those things that's still not that easy. We've all folded shirts, opened bags, assembled boxes, or handled food with both hands, and it seems easy to us. But all of these tasks require our two arms and hands to coordinate continuously, every little movement, and it's not just about where to move but when, and how much force to apply when grasping something.

To build better models for bimanual manipulation, we need to know which AI architectures are better suited for these tasks. Our AI research team spent time looking at the different AI architectures and wrote a comprehensive survey paper that reviews more than 200 papers and compares 31 vision-language-action (VLA) models.

Here's what we found:

As the coordination required between two arms increases, the way a model generates actions becomes a lot more important.

For loosely coupled tasks, many architectures perform well. But once two arms need to remain synchronized without pausing, architectures that generate actions for both arms jointly become much better suited than those that generate one arm after the other.

Flow-based action generation seems to offer one of the strongest trade-offs between coordinated action generation and the inference speed needed for real-time control.

Of course, architecture is just one piece of the puzzle. Our survey also highlights several areas where the field still needs to do significantly more research: better evaluation benchmarks specific to bimanual manipulation, richer sensing through force and tactile feedback, and the reliability and safety needed for robots to operate continuously in production environments.

I hope our paper can be a useful resource for researchers and engineers who work on robotic manipulation. Link to the full paper in comments!

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 month ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Placing food onto a tray, wrap, or bowl as it moves down a conveyor is one of those things that looks trivial at first glance but is way harder when you have to do it 110 million times with minimal errors across dozens of conveyors, plants, ingredients, trays, and users. Edge cases that seem very rare and have 0.001% probability show up hundreds of times. 

Our robots are also designed to work alongside humans, which means there's a lot of human-related randomness—people accelerating, decelerating, or stopping the conveyor, adding bowls at the last second, removing bowls, and bumping into bowls after we've already detected them. Randomness ensues! 

All of this randomness is handled by our on-device physical AI models. Our models track the conveyor, estimate conveyor velocity (which is harder than it seems since most conveyors aren't moving at stable speeds), detect each tray and compartment, and estimate the topology of each tray—all at once, at production speed.

Here's what's actually happening under the hood:

Our multi-camera system fuses RGB and depth data from multiple 3D sensors into a single point cloud of everything on the line—pans, conveyor, and bowls. The system continuously estimates the conveyor's 3D plane as it moves and simultaneously detects every meal tray on the line.

For each tray, our AI models infer its full 6-DoF pose and map it to a known tray topology. This lets us project each compartment's exact placement region from image space into the 3D workspace so the robot knows precisely where each compartment sits in the physical world, not just in a camera feed.

At the same time, the system is performing full pose estimation on every item in the source pan, so the robot knows how to pick each piece before it moves.

Getting every deposit right consistently at production speed is what we've spent years building.

author.name: Rajat Bhageria
author.info: Founder at Chef | Physical AI for the Food Industry

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
Food manufacturers care deeply about portion consistency. When a meal calls for 50 g of diced chicken, every meal needs to be as close to 50 g as possible—too little and the consumer is shortchanged, too much and the manufacturer is giving away product.

Chef robots estimate pick depth geometrically by computing the utensil's cross-sectional volume relative to the ingredient surface (essentially figuring out the volume swept by the tool). A feedback loop then corrects that estimate, pick by pick, based on the actual measured weight. This works well in production and delivers better-than-human consistency for most ingredients.

But we're always looking for ways to improve accuracy. Geometric models work by making simplifying assumptions about how food behaves, and we wanted to explore what a model could do if it learned ingredient behavior directly from data instead.

So we built CLUTCH—a neural network that ingests a point cloud of the ingredient surface and a target weight and learns to predict pick depth directly from real pick data rather than relying on geometric assumptions. When we tested it across a wide range of target weights, pick depth standard deviation dropped from 3.741 mm to 1.985 mm, and picks accurate within 2 mm went from 32.94% to 80.27%—without any closed-loop correction applied.

The next step is to make CLUTCH a single, generalized model trained across all Chef utensils and ingredients in production.

More on how we built it—link in comments.

posts.content:
Each time a Chef robot deposits food, its gripper must open at the right speed. Too fast and the food spills; too slow and the deposit is incomplete before the bowl moves on. The right speed differs for each ingredient.

The problem is that pneumatic grippers don't behave consistently. Pressure varies. Hardware ages. The same command produces different results on different robots, or even on the same robot over time. 

We tried the obvious fix: manually retuning per-gripper parameters. It worked, but it didn't scale.

So we built an AI-powered system that measures what the gripper actually does and automatically corrects for it.

We added a flowmeter to the pneumatic circuit—a small sensor that measures airflow on the exhaust side of the piston. That single addition made gripper behavior observable for the first time. Everything else followed from that.

From there, we stacked three techniques: regression to build a learned prior from characterization data, a neural network to detect when the gripper movement ends, and online adaptive control to update a per-gripper correction after each movement.

The top plot shows the flow signal as the gripper opens and closes. The bottom plot shows the neural network's confidence—it hits 99% (red dot) almost exactly at the true stop time (green).

Read more about how we built it on our engineering blog (link in comments)!

posts.content:
A lot of the debate in physical AI today focuses on generalist models and embodiments vs. vertical-specific ones.

But here's the thing: Our customers don't need a robot that can do every task in the world. They need a robot that can portion food with superhuman consistency, withstand cold storage and daily washdowns with buckets of hot water, integrate into production lines, and deliver clear ROI. 

In other words, customers don't want a "human" - they need a superhuman 𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘢𝘴𝘬.  

All of these food-specific components add cost to the BOM. That cost is completely unnecessary to incur and deploy in construction, where you need equipment that can withstand extreme heat (100F+) and heavy dust. And that construction-specific equipment you don’t need in a medical clean room to make a surgical robot. Each use case demands its own embodiment. 

That observation led us to a broader thesis: Intelligence will become increasingly shared. Embodiments will remain highly specialized.

The underlying physics of the world is the same everywhere, so knowledge can transfer across domains. But the economics, environments, and operational requirements of food, construction, logistics, healthcare, and manufacturing are very different.

That's why we believe the winning physical AI stack will look a lot like the modern software stack: open-source pre-trained models as a base with vertical-specific data for post-training, embodiment, and applications on top.

This pattern already exists in software. Companies like Glean, Harvey, Cursor, Sierra, and Decagon build on foundation models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and others.

It's also why I think some of the largest companies in physical AI won't necessarily be the companies building the generalist systems.

Labor is a ~$45 trillion market globally. Food alone is a multi-trillion-dollar industry. If you build the dominant AI platform for a major vertical, the opportunity is enormous.

That's the thesis we've been building Chef around. Read the full post (link in comments)!

posts.content:
One thing we've learned while building robots for the food industry is that the hardest problems are often the ones that look the simplest from the outside.

We've been placing ingredients into small compartments and inserts for a while. For most ingredients, our shielded utensils and vision system get the job done. But finer, stickier ingredients like cheese tend to 'fling' away when the utensil opens. 

There are two problems with this. The target area is very small, so there is almost no margin for error on a fast-moving line. Also, after picking up an ingredient, some of it may cling to the outer surface of the utensil and get stuck between utensils, landing in the wrong compartment while depositing.

We're now launching deposit assist to fix this. 

Deposit assist is a hardware attachment that food manufacturers can add directly to Chef's utensils in conjunction with Chef's Physical AI models to place into small inserts. It acts as a physical funnel to guide each deposit toward the center of the target compartment as the utensil opens. 

It also shakes the utensil multiple times over the pan before each deposit to get rid of any leftover ingredients stuck between the utensils, reducing spillage into adjacent compartments. We added a food-safe, NSF-certified air-cylinder actuator to the end-of-arm tool to control the utensil's shaking motion.

It works with our existing utensils without requiring changes to the production line. The guard geometry can be customized depending on the number of utensils, compartment type, and SKU.

More on our blog (link in comments)!

World models could change how we train robots: instead of learning only from actions taken in the real world (which is slow and expensive), world models let robots predict possible futures, learn tasks, and evaluate actions. And as VLAs are getting better at turning vision and language into robot actions, these two directions are converging into world-action models, which can both predict what happens next and generate the actions to get there.

The difficult part is that a plausible future doesn't necessarily follow the laws of physics. That might make or break world models for robotics, where physics is kind of everything.

Our team just published a survey of world models and world-action models that covers hundreds of research contributions and systems. We identified six major approaches and mapped out which one might be best suited for different domains (RL, robotics, autonomous driving, gaming, general-purpose simulation, and digital environments).

posts.content:
What does it actually take for a robot to pick up a chicken breast?

Our robots use piece-picking to handle discrete items like chicken breasts, pork chops, oranges, apples, cookies, and burger buns, picking each item individually from a pan and placing it precisely into a tray or packaging container.

Here's what's actually happening under the hood:

The pan is unstructured. Pieces are scattered at various angles, sometimes hidden by others, and at different depths. Chef robots can't just reach in and grab any piece.

→ So our AI-powered computer vision system first scans the entire pan, detects each individual piece, and segments the pieces in real time, even when items are irregularly distributed throughout the pan.

→ From there, our physical AI models compute a 3D pose estimate for every piece. Not just where it is, but exactly how it's oriented in space. This lets the robots decide how to approach each individual pick.

→ Then the robot makes an angled pick. It tilts the vacuum suction cup to match the surface orientation of the target piece for the best seal before lifting.

The result is consistent picks, even when pieces are partially hidden or scattered throughout the pan. No pre-sorting required.

This is what it looks like running live in production.
